entries.title: Scientific Computing Stack
entries.why: Context analysis requires heavy numerical computation: correlation matrices, z-scores, statistical tests. NumPy/Pandas/SciPy are the standard scientific Python stack for these operations.
entries.whatItDoes: Imports numpy for array math, pandas for DataFrames, scipy.stats for t-distribution p-values, psycopg2 for database queries, and the local config module.
entries.perfNotes: These libraries use C extensions under the hood - vectorized operations are fast

entries.title: 50 Sensor Columns Definition
entries.why: The analysis engine needs to know ALL 50 sensor parameters. Hard-coding them here ensures consistency with producer.py and enables category-based analysis (environmental vs mechanical vs thermal, etc.).
entries.whatItDoes: Defines SENSOR_COLUMNS list with 50 sensors in 5 categories (10 each): environmental, mechanical, thermal, electrical, fluid dynamics. SENSOR_CATEGORIES dict maps category names to their sensors for grouping analysis results.

failureModes.condition: Producer adds new sensor not in this list
failureModes.behavior: New sensor ignored in correlation/pattern analysis
failureModes.recovery: Keep this list synchronized with producer.py manually

entries.perfNotes: Class-level constants avoid repeated list creation

entries.title: Analyzer Initialization
entries.why: The window_size determines how many readings before/after an anomaly to fetch for context. This affects both query performance (larger windows = more data) and analysis quality (more context = better correlation detection).
entries.whatItDoes: Accepts optional window_size parameter, defaults to config.CONTEXT_WINDOW_SIZE if not provided. Stores instance logger for error tracking.
entries.perfNotes: Window size impacts DB query cost - 50 readings before + 50 after = 101 rows per analysis

entries.title: Context Window Fetcher (3 Queries)
entries.why: To understand WHY an anomaly occurred, you need context: what were the sensor values leading up to it? What happened after? This fetches a window of readings centered on the anomaly.
entries.whatItDoes: Executes 3 SQL queries: (1) fetch the anomaly reading by ID, (2) fetch window_size readings BEFORE by ID DESC, (3) fetch window_size readings AFTER by ID ASC. Returns dict with 'before', 'anomaly', 'after' DataFrames. Note: before_rows is reversed to chronological order.

failureModes.recovery: Caller should check for None return
Retry logic should be at calling layer

tests.what: Test with reading at dataset start
tests.how: Pass reading_id=1, verify before DataFrame is empty

entries.perfNotes: 3 sequential queries - could be combined with UNION but readability matters more here
entries.securityNotes: Uses parameterized queries (%s) - safe from SQL injection

entries.title: Pearson Correlation with P-Values
entries.why: Finding which sensors move together helps identify root cause. If temperature and bearing_temp are highly correlated during an anomaly, they might share a common cause (overheating). P-values filter out spurious correlations from small samples.
entries.whatItDoes: Concatenates before+anomaly+after into one DataFrame. Computes 50x50 Pearson correlation matrix. For each pair: calculates t-statistic and p-value from scipy.stats.t.cdf. Filters to |r|>0.5 AND p<0.05. Labels as 'strong' (>0.7) or 'moderate'. Returns top 20 sorted by absolute correlation.

failureModes.recovery: Need minimum sample size for meaningful correlation

failureModes.condition: All values identical for a sensor

entries.perfNotes: O(n^2) for 50 sensors = 1225 unique pairs - fast enough

entries.title: Z-Score Anomaly Scoring
entries.why: Z-scores tell us 'how unusual is this value compared to recent baseline?' A z-score of 3 means the value is 3 standard deviations from the mean - extremely rare if data is normally distributed (~0.3% chance).
entries.whatItDoes: For each of 50 sensors: computes baseline mean/std from 'before' readings, calculates z-score of anomaly value, computes percent change, determines trend direction from last 3 readings, adds category and unit metadata. Sorts by |z_score| descending. Groups results by sensor category.

failureModes.condition: No baseline readings (anomaly at dataset start)
failureModes.recovery: Need historical data for baseline comparison
Constant values aren't anomalous by definition

entries.perfNotes: Linear scan through 50 sensors - very fast

entries.title: Complete Analysis Summary Generator
entries.why: This is the main entry point for external callers. It orchestrates context fetching, correlation analysis, and pattern identification into a single JSON-serializable result ready for ChatGPT or the UI.
entries.whatItDoes: Calls get_context_window(), compute_correlations(), identify_anomalous_patterns() in sequence. Converts Pandas DataFrames to dicts using to_dict('records'). Converts timestamps to strings for JSON serialization. Returns complete analysis package with reading_id, context, correlations, patterns, detected_sensors.
entries.perfNotes: Full analysis takes ~50ms including DB queries

entries.title: Anomaly Details Lookup Function
entries.why: The anomaly_detections table stores what the ML detected. This helper fetches those details so we know which sensors triggered the alert and what detection method (rule-based, Isolation Forest, LSTM) flagged it.
entries.whatItDoes: Standalone function (not a class method) that queries anomaly_detections by ID. Returns dict with: id, reading_id (foreign key to sensor_readings), detection_method, anomaly_score, is_anomaly flag, detected_sensors array, created_at timestamp.
entries.perfNotes: Single indexed lookup by primary key - very fast
